United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)

title.narrative: UNESCO’s multi-hazards and multisectoral disaster response for build back better

description.narrative:
UNESCO has a Heritage Emergency Fund, and the Education Sector also deploys funding for emergency response. With these resources UNESCO sends the experts to support the situation through their expertise to address the issue relayed to education and culture, however, Natural Sciences Sector does not have dedicated resources for emergency response. Due to the lack of a dedicated fund for emergency response in Natural Sciences Sector, it is difficult to send experts for the multi-sectoral missions once disasters happen.
“Early warning systems” and “Preparedness and Response” are critical components of disaster resilience building, providing vital information to help communities prepare and mitigate the impacts of natural hazards, ultimately saving lives, reducing damage and losses. It is the key to shift from post-disaster response to proactive disaster risk reduction as highlighted in Sendai Framework 2015 through the improved Early warning systems and Preparedness and Response. Therefore, one of the main objectives of the fund for emergency response is to support countries/regions to recover and reconstruct from the damage quickly.
UNESCO is dedicated to supporting Member States in strengthening their capabilities to establish, maintain and enhance early warning systems to align with the objectives in the Sendai Framework. The ambitious vision set forth by the Secretary-General to ensure universal access to early warning systems by 2027 is one in which UNESCO actively participates. UNESCO is the only UN Agency which covers both hydrological (flood and drought) and geological/geophysical hazards (tsunami, earthquake and landslide) in its programme for disaster risk reduction.
